mainTopic: The stages of mourning for an אבל: working, greetings, comforting over thirty days and twelve months, and a latecomer's count of שבעה
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier question: an אבל puts on תפילין even in the first three days, because a מצוה is different. Then three ברייתות show that the first three days of mourning are the strictest, with rules about working, visiting another mourner, and greeting people. The story of רבי עקיבא blessing the crowd on the day his sons died seems to contradict the greeting rule, but the גמרא answers that honoring the public is different. Next, a ברייתא forbidding greetings for thirty days seems to clash with the seven-day rule. רב אידי בר אבין explains that the mourner may greet others after seven days, but others may not greet him for thirty. A ברייתא about twelve months, with רבי מאיר's parable of the doctor who breaks a healed leg, is explained as applying to a parent, while the shorter time applies to other relatives. Finally, a ברייתא teaches when a mourner who arrives late counts שבעה with the family, and רבי יוחנן adds that this applies only when the head of the household is home. A new question is introduced at the very end, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A מצוה is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers an earlier question: an אבל puts on תפילין even during the first three days because תפילין is a מצוה, and a מצוה is treated differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: A מצוה is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering the question just asked: why may an אבל put on תפילין even though the first three days carry heavy restrictions? The answer is that a מצוה is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The restrictions of the first three days cover ordinary activities. Putting on תפילין is an obligation from the תורה, so those restrictions do not push it aside. This settles the apparent contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: A commandment; here, putting on תפילין
תפילין, which the earlier discussion was about

phrases.english: A מצוה is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised just before this section about תפילין during the first three days of mourning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: a מצוה obligation differs from the ordinary activities the first three days restrict.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought the strictness of the first three days would forbid even תפילין.
steps.terutzMaskana: תפילין is a מצוה, so the restrictions of the first three days do not apply to it.

steps.title: A mourner and working
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that an אבל may not do מלאכה (work) for the first three days, even a poor person living on צדקה. After that he may work privately at home, and a woman may spin at home.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: For the first three days a mourner is forbidden to work, even a poor man who lives on charity. From then on, he may work privately inside his home. And a woman may spin with a spindle inside her home.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about when an אבל may go back to work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first three days are fully closed to work, with no exception even for someone in real financial need. From the fourth day, a person may work, but only quietly at home, out of public view. Spinning at home is given as an example of this kind of private work for a woman.

keyTerms.meaning: A poor person supported by charity
A spindle used for spinning thread

steps.confusionAlert: From the fourth day the work is allowed only privately at home. It does not mean an אבל may go back to working openly.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A mourner, during the first three days,
is forbidden to work,
even a poor person who is supported by charity.

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ — עוֹשֶׂה בְּצִינְעָא בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ.
phrases.english: From here on, he may work privately inside his home.
And a woman may spin with a spindle inside her home.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new series of ברייתות about the stages of mourning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No work at all during the first three days, even for a poor person. Afterward, only private work at home is permitted.

steps.title: A mourner visiting another mourner
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that during his first three days an אבל does not go to comfort another mourner. After that he may go, but he sits with the mourners, not with the comforters.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: For the first three days a mourner does not go to a house of mourning. From then on he may go, but he does not sit in the place of the comforters, only in the place of those being comforted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא, this one about whether an אבל may go comfort someone else who is mourning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the first three days he stays home entirely. Afterward he may visit, but he is still a mourner himself, so he sits among the people being comforted. He does not sit among the comforters.

keyTerms.meaning: Comforters, the people visiting the mourners

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A mourner, during the first three days,
does not go to a house of mourning,
from here on, he may go,
but he does not sit in the place of the comforters,
rather in the place of those being comforted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ברייתא that uses the same three-day structure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No visiting other mourners in the first three days. Afterward he may visit, but he sits among the mourners.

steps.title: A mourner and greeting people
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the rules of שאילת שלום for an אבל. In the first three days he does not greet anyone. From day three to day seven he may answer a greeting but not start one. After that he greets and answers normally.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: For the first three days a mourner may not greet others. From the third to the seventh day, he answers but does not initiate. From then on, he greets and answers as usual.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third ברייתא, this one about saying "שלום" to people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא has three stages instead of two. In the first three days there is no greeting at all. From the third to the seventh day, he may only reply when someone else greets him. After the seventh day, everything is back to normal.

keyTerms.meaning: Greeting someone, asking after their well-being

steps.whatToRemember: All three ברייתות follow the same pattern. The first three days are the strictest, and the restrictions loosen in stages afterward. For greetings there is a middle stage, days three to seven, when he may only answer.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A mourner, during the first three days,
is forbidden to greet others.
From the third until the seventh day,
he answers but does not initiate a greeting.
From here on,
he greets and answers in his usual way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third parallel ברייתא that adds a middle stage, from day three to day seven.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Days one to three: no greeting at all. Days three to seven: he may answer but not initiate. After the seventh day: he greets and answers normally.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא greeted the crowd on the day his sons died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule that an אבל may not greet anyone in the first three days, using the story of רבי עקיבא, who blessed the crowd with 'go in peace' right after his sons died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is an אבל really forbidden to greet people during the first three days? But a ברייתא teaches: רבי עקיבא's sons died, and all of Israel came and gave them a great הספד. When the people were leaving, רבי עקיבא stood on a big bench and said: 'Our brothers, house of Israel, listen! Even if my two sons had been grooms, I would be comforted by the honor you showed. If you came for עקיבא himself, there are many people named עקיבא in the market. Rather, you said to yourselves: the תורה of his God is in his heart. So your reward is double. Go to your homes in peace!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the rule from Step 4 by bringing a story where an אבל on his very first day did say 'go in peace' to people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said an אבל does not greet anyone in the first three days. Yet רבי עקיבא, on the day of the funeral, ended his speech with 'לכו לבתיכם לשלום', which is a greeting. So the story seems to contradict the rule.
steps.confusionAlert: The words בשעת פטירתן do not mean when the sons died. They mean when the crowd was getting ready to leave.

phrases.english: During the first three days
is he forbidden to greet people?
But it was taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲשֶׂה וּמֵתוּ בָּנָיו שֶׁל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
phrases.english: There was a case where the sons of Rabbi Akiva died
all of Israel came in
and eulogized them with a great eulogy.
When they were taking leave
phrases.notes: This is talking about the crowd leaving, not about the sons passing away.

phrases.aramaic: עָמַד רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא עַל סַפְסָל גָּדוֹל
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva stood on a large bench
and said: Our brothers, the house of Israel, listen!
Even if the two sons had been grooms
he would be comforted because of the honor you have shown.
phrases.notes: רבי עקיבא is talking about himself here, as if about someone else.

phrases.english: And if you came for the sake of Akiva
there are many Akivas in the marketplace.
Rather, this is what you said:
"The Torah of his God is in his heart."
All the more so, your reward is doubled
Go to your homes in peace!

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים אָסוּר בִּשְׁאֵילַת שָׁלוֹם? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first-three-days rule from Step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that an אבל may not greet anyone during the first three days.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי עקיבא, as an אבל on the day of the funeral, said 'go to your homes in peace,' which is a greeting.

steps.title: Honoring the public is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי עקיבא's greeting was allowed because showing respect to a large public is a special case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Honor of the public is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: רבי עקיבא's case was special because he was showing respect to a huge crowd.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule from Step 4 still stands. When a big crowd comes to honor the אבל, he may greet them out of respect for them. This is an exception, not a cancellation of the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Honor or respect for the public

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the greeting rule for an אבל can give way when respect for a large public is involved.

phrases.english: Respect for the public is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא's greeting would show that an אבל may greet anyone in the first three days.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule stays. Greeting a large crowd out of respect for them is an exception.

steps.title: Quoting the days three-to-seven rule again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the ברייתא again: from day three to day seven the אבל answers greetings but does not start them, and after that he acts normally.
steps.simpleTranslation: From the third day until the seventh, he answers but does not start a greeting. From then on, he greets and answers as usual.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the next line of the ברייתא from Step 4 again. It is setting up a closer look at this part of the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having finished with the first three days, the גמרא now moves to the second part of the ברייתא. This is not a new rule. The line is being brought back so the גמרא can discuss it next.

phrases.english: From the third day until the seventh
he answers but does not start a greeting
From then on
he greets and answers in his usual way.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה וְעַד שִׁבְעָה מֵשִׁיב וְאֵינוֹ שׁוֹאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא from Step 4 to look at its next clause.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From day three to seven an אבל answers greetings but does not start them; after seven he greets and answers normally.

steps.title: A second source seems to forbid greeting a mourner for thirty days
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא saying that for thirty days you comfort an אבל but do not greet him. This contradicts the ברייתא that allowed normal greetings after seven days.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the גמרא raises a contradiction from another ברייתא: If someone meets his friend who is a mourner within thirty days, he speaks words of comfort to him but does not greet him. After thirty days, he greets him but does not speak words of comfort to him. If the man's wife died and he married another woman, one may not go into his house to comfort him. If he meets him in the market, he speaks to him softly and seriously.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets one ברייתא against another. The first one (step 7) said greetings go back to normal after seven days. This one says no greetings for thirty days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ברייתא allowed normal greetings from day eight. This ברייתא says that within thirty days you only comfort the mourner and do not greet him. The two time limits, seven and thirty, seem to clash. The line about the man who remarried is just the rest of the same ברייתא and is not part of the challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And contrast them': the גמרא sets one source against another to show a contradiction
The first thirty days of mourning
Words of comfort for a mourner
Greets him (literally, asks about his welfare)
Softly and seriously, in a low-key way

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. It challenges the seven-day rule from step 7, which said that after day seven the אבל greets and answers like everyone else.

phrases.english: And contrast them (raise a contradiction):
phrases.notes: The other side of the contradiction is the ברייתא from step 7, which allowed normal greetings after seven days.

phrases.english: One who finds his friend in mourning,
within thirty days
speaks words of comfort with him
but does not greet him;
after thirty days
he greets him
but does not speak words of comfort with him.
If his wife died and he married another woman,
one is not allowed to enter his house
to speak words of comfort with him.
If he found him in the marketplace,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹמֵר לוֹ בְּשָׂפָה רָפָה וּבְכוֹבֶד רֹאשׁ.
phrases.english: he speaks to him with a soft voice and a serious manner.
phrases.notes: Literally 'with a weak lip and a heavy head': quiet and low-key, not a cheerful hello.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule in step 7 that greetings go back to normal after seven days.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that after seven days the אבל greets and is greeted normally
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא forbids greeting a mourner for thirty days, which clashes with a seven-day limit.

steps.title: The mourner may greet others, but others may not greet him
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין explains that the two sources talk about different people. After seven days the אבל may greet others. For thirty days, others may not greet the אבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said: The mourner himself may greet others, because the others are at peace. Others may not greet him, because he is not at peace.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אידי בר אבין settles the contradiction by showing that each ברייתא is about a different direction of greeting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seven-day ברייתא is about the אבל greeting other people, which he may do once the seven days end. The thirty-day ברייתא is about other people greeting the אבל, which is still not allowed. The reason is a play on שלום: others are at peace, so wishing them peace fits, but the mourner is not at peace, so wishing it to him does not.

keyTerms.meaning: Other people, meaning those who are not mourners

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule ends up running in two directions. From day eight the mourner may greet others, but others still do not greet him until thirty days are over.

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said:
He (the mourner) greets others
because others are at peace;
others do not greet him
because he is not at peace.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source talks about a different person doing the greeting
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to give one rule about greeting a mourner, with two different time limits.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seven days applies to the mourner greeting others. Thirty days applies to others greeting the mourner.

steps.title: If no one may greet him, why does he 'answer' greetings?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the earlier ברייתא says the אבל 'answers' greetings during days three to seven. That suggests people do greet him, which goes against רב אידי בר אבין.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the ברייתא teaches that he 'answers,' this implies that people do greet him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אידי בר אבין's answer using the wording of the earlier ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said that from day three to day seven the אבל answers greetings. You can only answer a greeting if someone greeted you first. So it seems others are allowed to greet him, which goes against the claim that others may not greet him for thirty days.

phrases.english: But from the fact that it teaches 'he answers,'
phrases.notes: This points back to the ברייתא in step 7: from day three to day seven he answers but does not start a greeting.

phrases.english: it follows that we do greet him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אידי בר אבין's rule that others may not greet the mourner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Answering a greeting assumes someone greeted him, so it seems people are allowed to greet him.

steps.title: The people greeting him did not know he was mourning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about people who greeted him without knowing he was an אבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about people who did not know he was a mourner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in step 10 and keeps רב אידי בר אבין's rule in place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People are still not allowed to greet a mourner. But if someone greets him without knowing he is mourning, he may answer. So 'he answers' does not mean greeting him is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: After seven days the אבל may greet others. Others may not knowingly greet him until thirty days are over. If people greet him without knowing, he may answer them.

phrases.english: It is where they did not know.
phrases.notes: Meaning they did not know he was a mourner, so they greeted him by mistake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to people who greeted him without knowing
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'He answers' seemed to show that people may greet a mourner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answering only happens when people greet him without knowing he is mourning, so the ban on knowingly greeting him still stands.

steps.title: Then the first three days should be the same
steps.stepSummary: If the ברייתא is talking about people who did not know he was an אבל, the same should apply in the first three days.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then there too he should be allowed to answer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave in step 11. If the אבל may answer people who did not know he was mourning, he should also be allowed to answer them during the first three days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said that in the first three days the אבל does not answer greetings at all. If the reason he may answer on days three to seven is that the people did not know he was mourning, that reason works just as well on days one to three. So why does the ברייתא treat the two periods differently?

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is how you explain it
There too; the same should apply in the other case

phrases.english: If so, there too [he should answer]!
phrases.notes: "There" means the first three days of mourning, when the ברייתא said he does not answer greetings at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 11 by applying its logic to the first three days.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 11 that the ברייתא is talking about people who did not know he was an אבל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If not knowing is the reason he may answer, the same reason should let him answer during the first three days, yet the ברייתא forbids it.

steps.title: In the first three days he must tell them; later he need not
steps.stepSummary: During the first three days the אבל must tell people he is mourning and must not answer. After that he does not need to tell them, so he may answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, in the first three days, he tells them he is mourning and does not answer them. Here, after three days, he does not need to tell them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing a real difference between the two time periods. In the first three days the אבל must speak up and say he is mourning, but later he may just answer the greeting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both periods involve people who did not know he was an אבל. The difference is what the אבל must do about it. In the first three days, when mourning is at its strongest, he must tell them and not answer. From day three to seven he may simply answer without explaining.

keyTerms.meaning: He lets them know (that he is mourning)

steps.whatToRemember: First three days: the אבל tells people he is mourning and does not answer greetings. Days three to seven: he may answer people who greeted him without knowing, and he does not need to explain.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם — מוֹדַע לְהוּ וְלָא מַהְדַּר לְהוּ,
phrases.english: There, he informs them and does not answer them;
phrases.notes: "There" is the first three days of mourning.

phrases.english: here, he does not need to inform them.
phrases.notes: "Here" is day three to day seven. Since he does not have to tell them, he may simply answer.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם — מוֹדַע לְהוּ וְלָא מַהְדַּר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between the two time periods by what the אבל must do
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two periods should be the same, since in both the people did not know he was mourning.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the first three days the אבל must tell people and not answer. Afterwards he need not tell them and may answer.

steps.title: A ברייתא says not to greet an אבל for twelve months
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא saying you may not greet an אבל for twelve months. This contradicts the earlier ruling that limits it to thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: A contradiction is raised: If someone finds his friend mourning within twelve months, he speaks words of comfort to him but does not greet him. After twelve months he greets him and does not speak words of comfort, but he may speak to him indirectly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new contradiction. A ברייתא says others may not greet an אבל for a full twelve months, but the earlier source (step 8, explained in step 9) set that limit at thirty days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב אידי בר אבין, others may not greet the אבל for thirty days. This ברייתא stretches that ban to twelve months, which is much longer. It also adds that after twelve months you should not comfort him openly, only in an indirect way.

keyTerms.meaning: And they raised a contradiction between sources
Greets him; asks how he is

phrases.english: And they contradicted it: One who finds his friend mourning,
within twelve months,
speaks words of comfort with him,
and does not greet him.

phrases.aramaic: לְאַחַר שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ — שׁוֹאֵל בִּשְׁלוֹמוֹ,
phrases.english: After twelve months, he greets him,
and does not speak words of comfort with him,
but he may speak with him indirectly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new contradiction against the thirty-day limit set up in steps 8 and 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that others may not greet the אבל for thirty days
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says greetings are forbidden for twelve months, not thirty days.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's parable: the doctor who breaks a healed leg
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר compares comforting an אבל after twelve months to a doctor who breaks a healed leg just to show off his medicines.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר said: Someone who finds his friend mourning after twelve months and speaks words of comfort to him, what is he like? He is like a person whose leg broke and healed. A doctor found him and said: Come to me, so I can break it and heal it, so that you will know my medicines are good.
steps.whatsHappening: This is still part of the same ברייתא. רבי מאיר explains with a parable why you should not openly comfort an אבל after twelve months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After a year the pain has begun to heal. Openly comforting him reopens the wound just so you can soothe it again, like a doctor breaking a healed leg. This explains the ברייתא's rule that after twelve months you speak to him only indirectly.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it like? (opens a parable)

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir said:

phrases.aramaic: הַמּוֹצֵא אֶת חֲבֵרוֹ אָבֵל לְאַחַר שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ,
phrases.english: One who finds his friend mourning after twelve months,

phrases.aramaic: וּמְדַבֵּר עִמּוֹ תַּנְחוּמִין, לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה?
phrases.english: and speaks words of comfort with him, what is he like?
Like a person whose leg broke and healed,
a doctor found him and said to him:
Come to me, so I can break it and heal it,
so that you will know that my medicines are good!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר: הַמּוֹצֵא אֶת חֲבֵרוֹ אָבֵל לְאַחַר שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted in step 14 and gives the reason for its rule after twelve months.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Openly comforting an אבל after twelve months reopens a healed wound and should not be done.

steps.title: Twelve months for a parent, less for other relatives
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the twelve-month rule applies to mourning for a father or mother, and the shorter rule applies to other relatives.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about his father and mother, and that one is about other relatives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction from step 14. Each source is talking about a different kind of loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mourning for a father or mother lasts longer, so others may not greet the אבל for twelve months. For other relatives the mourning is shorter, so the shorter limit applies. Both sources are correct, each for its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

steps.whatToRemember: Others may not greet an אבל for twelve months when he lost a parent, and for a shorter time when he lost another relative.
steps.confusionAlert: The twelve-month rule does not cancel the thirty-day rule. They are two separate rules for two different kinds of loss.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is about his father and mother,
phrases.notes: "This" is the twelve-month ברייתא from step 14.

phrases.english: that is about other relatives.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּאָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ, הָא בִּשְׁאָר קְרוֹבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources into different cases (which relative died)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources argue about how long others may not greet an אבל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Twelve months applies to mourning for a parent. The shorter period applies to other relatives.

steps.title: Why not allow indirect comfort for other relatives too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why, in the case of other relatives after thirty days, one cannot at least offer תנחומין in an indirect way.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, in the case of other relatives after thirty days, let him speak words of comfort to him indirectly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ruling that after thirty days, for other relatives, you do not speak תנחומין to the אבל. Why not at least comfort him indirectly?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 16 said the shorter time limit applies to relatives other than a parent. The ברייתא said that after that time you do not speak תנחומין at all. The גמרא asks whether that is too strict, since a softer, indirect kind of comfort would not reopen the wound.

keyTerms.meaning: There, meaning in that other case
Words of comfort for a mourner
From the side, meaning indirectly and not head-on

phrases.english: There too,
phrases.notes: "There" means the other relatives from step 16, once the thirty days are over.

phrases.english: let him speak words of comfort to him indirectly?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי, יְדַבֵּר עִמּוֹ תַּנְחוּמִין מִן הַצַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling for other relatives that came out of the answer in step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: The statement that after thirty days, for other relatives, one does not speak תנחומין to the אבל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Indirect comfort does not reopen the pain, so it should be allowed here as well.

steps.title: Yes, indirect comfort is allowed; only the normal kind is not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees. The ברייתא only forbids comfort in the usual direct way. Indirect comfort is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, it is indeed so. And what does it mean when it says he does not speak words of comfort to him? It means in his usual way. But he may speak with him indirectly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge and explains the ברייתא more narrowly. The ban is only on regular, direct comfort.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing in the ruling is taken back. The words "does not speak תנחומין" are now read as "does not speak תנחומין in the normal way." Indirect comfort stays allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes, that is indeed so (the גמרא agrees with the question)

phrases.english: Yes, it is indeed so.
And what does "he does not speak words of comfort to him" mean?
In his usual way,
but he may speak with him indirectly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין הָכִי נָמֵי. וּמַאי אֵינוֹ מְדַבֵּר עִמּוֹ תַּנְחוּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of step 17 and reads the ברייתא more narrowly
steps.terutzResolutionType: Agreement plus a narrower reading of the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to forbid any comfort at all after thirty days.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only normal, direct comfort is forbidden. Indirect comfort is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: After the main mourning time, you do not comfort an אבל in the normal direct way, but indirect comfort is always allowed.

steps.title: A mourner who arrives late: when he counts with the family
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches when a late-arriving אבל joins the family's count of שבעה and when he counts his own seven days. רבי שמעון is more lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A mourner who comes during the first three days from a nearby place counts with the others. If he comes from a far place, he counts on his own. After that, even if he comes from a nearby place, he counts on his own. רבי שמעון says: even if he comes on the seventh day from a nearby place, he counts with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא. It deals with a family member who was not there at first and arrives during שבעה. Does he finish with everyone else, or start his own seven days?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two things matter: when he arrives (within the first three days or later) and from where (near or far). Only near plus within three days lets him join the family's count. רבי שמעון lets someone from nearby join even on the seventh day.

keyTerms.meaning: He counts with them, so he finishes שבעה when they do
He counts for himself, a full seven days of his own
A nearby place / a far place

steps.confusionAlert: Counting "with them" is the easier result, because he may end up mourning fewer than seven days. Counting "on his own" means a full seven days.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A mourner, during the first three days,
if he came from a nearby place, he counts with them,
phrases.notes: "Them" means the other mourners at home. He finishes when they finish.

phrases.english: if he came from a far place, he counts on his own.
From here onward,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ בָּא מִמָּקוֹם קָרוֹב — מוֹנֶה לְעַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: even if he came from a nearby place, he counts on his own.
Rabbi Shimon says:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ בָּא בְּיוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי מִמָּקוֹם קָרוֹב —
phrases.english: Even if he came on the seventh day from a nearby place,
he counts with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אָבֵל, שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: counting שבעה for a mourner who arrives late
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Within the first three days, a mourner from nearby counts with the family; otherwise he counts his own seven days. רבי שמעון lets someone from nearby join the family's count even on the seventh day.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main source for the practical rule about a relative who arrives in the middle of שבעה.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's condition: the head of the household must be home
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the first rule of the ברייתא. Then רבי יוחנן limits it: it only applies when the main member of the family is at home.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: In the first three days, if he came from a nearby place, he counts with them. רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: This is only when the head of the household is in the house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first ruling of the ברייתא again so that it can add a condition. רבי יוחנן says the late arrival joins the family's count only if the family's main person is at home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the family's mourning follows the main person of the house. A late arrival can join that count. But if the main person is the one arriving late, he does not follow the others and counts his own seven days.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is only when..., which adds a condition
The main or head member of the household

phrases.english: The Master said:
During the first three days,
if he came from a nearby place, he counts with them.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
And this is only when the head of the household is in the house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the first ruling of the ברייתא from step 19 and adds a limiting condition
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A mourner who arrives late joins the family's count only if the head of the household is at home.

steps.title: A new question is raised
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא announces that the scholars had a question. The question itself comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was raised before them:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is about to ask a new question, probably building on רבי יוחנן's condition, and the actual question follows in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ signals a real open question, not an attack. Nothing has been asked yet. The learner should get ready for a new case.

keyTerms.meaning: It was asked of them; it introduces an open question among the scholars

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets up a new question that follows רבי יוחנן's condition
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Not stated yet. The question itself follows right after this line.
